You are the one responsible for knowing when you are not fit to drive, and that responsibility shapes everything that follows. Even a little alcohol may affect your driving, so the guide's advice is simple: if you plan to drink, hand the keys to someone who has not been drinking. The guide lists the ways it works against a driver. Alcohol can cause drowsiness. It weakens concentration and attention. It brings poorer coordination and poorer comprehension. And it leads to worse decisions. Look at that list as a whole: alertness, focus, control and judgment are all on it, and alcohol can bring every one of them. That is why the guide treats alcohol as one of the things that can weaken your driving, alongside drugs, even medicine, and simply being tired. It is also why the guide places the duty on you. That is why the guide's advice starts before the first drink. Even a little alcohol may affect your driving, so if you plan to drink, hand the keys to someone who has not been drinking. Your Blood Alcohol Content, or BAC, is written as a percent. In Missouri it is illegal to drive with a BAC of zero point zero eight percent or more. That is the limit for most drivers. Commercial vehicle drivers are held to a lower level, zero point zero four percent. Drivers under twenty-one are held to the lowest level of all, zero point zero two percent. So the legal BAC limit depends on the driver. Before you can say whether a BAC is legal, you need to know who was driving: a typical adult, a commercial vehicle driver, or someone under twenty-one. The same reading can be legal for one driver and illegal for another.","fact_ids":["sec12-F41","sec12-R01","sec12-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":48,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Not only alcohol","fact_ids":["sec12-F39","sec12-F40"]},"lines":[{"text":"DWI covers illegal drugs and medicine too.","fact_ids":["sec12-F39","sec12-F40"]},{"text":"Prescription and over-the-counter both count.","fact_ids":["sec12-F39","sec12-F40"]},{"text":"Same penalties, whatever caused it.","fact_ids":["sec12-F39","sec12-F40"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap that catches many drivers. People tend to think of DWI as an alcohol offense only. In Missouri you can be charged with DWI for driving impaired by alcohol, illegal drugs, prescription medicine, over-the-counter medicine, or any mix of them. Missouri law does not separate prescription, over-the-counter and illegal drugs. A medicine from your own doctor is treated no differently from an illegal drug when it comes to impaired driving. And the DWI penalties are the same whether alcohol or drugs caused the impairment. So an answer that offers a lighter penalty because the medicine was prescribed is wrong, and so is an answer that says only alcohol can lead to DWI.","fact_ids":["sec12-F39","sec12-F40"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":46,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check: medicine and DWI","fact_ids":["sec12-F39","sec12-F40"]},"lines":[{"text":"Jordan's prescribed medicine impaired his driving.","fact_ids":["sec12-F39","sec12-F40"]},{"text":"Can he be charged with DWI?","fact_ids":["sec12-F39","sec12-F40"]},{"text":"Are the penalties lighter?","fact_ids":["sec12-F39","sec12-F40"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: Jordan took a medicine his doctor prescribed for him, and it impaired his driving on the way home. The answer is yes, he can be charged, and no, the penalties are not lighter. In Missouri, DWI covers driving impaired by prescription medicine, as well as alcohol, illegal drugs, over-the-counter medicine or any mix. The law does not separate prescription, over-the-counter and illegal drugs, and the DWI penalties are the same whether alcohol or drugs caused the impairment.","fact_ids":["sec12-F39","sec12-F40"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Know the limit, know yourself","fact_ids":["sec12-F41","sec12-R01","sec12-F42","sec12-F01","sec12-F39"]},"lines":[{"text":"Limits: zero point zero eight, zero point zero four, zero point zero two.","fact_ids":["sec12-F41","sec12-R01","sec12-F42","sec12-F01","sec12-F39"]},{"text":"One drink probably affects you.","fact_ids":["sec12-F41","sec12-R01","sec12-F42","sec12-F01","sec12-F39"]},{"text":"DWI covers drugs and medicine.","fact_ids":["sec12-F41","sec12-R01","sec12-F42","sec12-F01","sec12-F39"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close this lesson, pull the pieces together. Then Missouri can act against an impaired driver in two separate ways, administrative actions and court-convicted actions, and each has its own penalties. In this lesson we look at the field tests, the chemical test and the cost of refusing it, then the notice the officer gives you on the administrative side, the hearing you can ask for, and two time periods that are easy to mix up.","fact_ids":["sec12-F04","sec12-F05","sec12-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":46,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Field tests, then chemical test","fact_ids":["sec12-F04","sec12-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Field tests: heel to toe, one-leg balance.","fact_ids":["sec12-F04","sec12-F05"]},{"text":"They help decide the arrest.","fact_ids":["sec12-F04","sec12-F05"]},{"text":"After arrest: breath, blood or urine test.","fact_ids":["sec12-F04","sec12-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Start with the field tests. Keep the order straight: field tests come before the arrest and guide that decision, and the chemical test comes after the arrest and gives the BAC level. So refusal carries its own penalty, separate from whatever a BAC result might have shown. If your BAC is zero point zero eight percent or more, or zero point zero two percent or more for a minor, the officer takes your license and gives you a notice. That notice says your license will be suspended or revoked after fifteen days. So the officer's notice is where the administrative track begins. You may keep driving legally until fifteen days after the hearing decision is mailed to you. So read the notice carefully. Whether a permit is included depends on the officer's mark, and whether you get the extra driving time depends on asking for a hearing and having it granted.","fact_ids":["sec12-F08","sec12-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u02-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Two fifteen-day periods","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F07","sec12-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"After the notice: license lost in fifteen days.","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F07","sec12-F09"]},{"text":"With a hearing: drive until fifteen days after the mailed decision.","fact_ids":["sec12-R02","sec12-F07","sec12-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap in this lesson. The other fifteen-day period on the notice page counts from the notice itself, when the license is suspended or revoked fifteen days after the notice. Administrative actions and court-convicted actions are separate, and each has its own penalties. On the administrative side, a chart sets penalties for a first offense and for a second offense within five years. On the court side, a judge's guilty finding starts a ladder of license actions that climbs from a ninety-day suspension for a first offense up to a ten-year denial for a third offense and any later one. We will work through each rung, and then look at a trap where a second offense means different things on the two tracks.","fact_ids":["sec12-F06","sec12-F10","sec12-F12","sec12-F19","sec12-F21"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The administrative chart","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-F11"]},"lines":[{"text":"First offense: license suspension.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-F11"]},{"text":"Second within five years: one-year revocation.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-F11"]},{"text":"Asterisk: interlock before reinstatement.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-F11"]}],"narration":{"text":"Start with the administrative chart. So the chart has two levels, and the second level depends on the five-year window. Some entries on the chart are marked with an asterisk. That mark has a specific meaning: an asterisk entry requires an Ignition Interlock Device to be installed before the license is reinstated. In other words, for those entries, getting your license back is not just a matter of serving the suspension or revocation. The device has to be in place first. We look at how an interlock works in a later lesson.","fact_ids":["sec12-F10","sec12-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":46,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec12-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"After a guilty finding","fact_ids":["sec12-F12","sec12-F13","sec12-F41"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop once the ticket reaches the Department.","fact_ids":["sec12-F12","sec12-F13","sec12-F41"]},{"text":"You are told by mail.","fact_ids":["sec12-F12","sec12-F13","sec12-F41"]},{"text":"Your record decides; points are added.","fact_ids":["sec12-F12","sec12-F13","sec12-F41"]}],"narration":{"text":"Now the court track. If a judge finds you guilty of DWI, or of a BAC of zero point zero eight percent or more, you can no longer drive legally once the ticket reaches the Department. You are not left guessing about the date. You are told by mail when to stop driving. What happens to the license then depends on your past driving record.
